notes.meaning: Paul travelled back to Derbe and then to Lystra, where he had planted churches on an earlier journey. There he met a young disciple named Timothy. Timothy's mother was a Jewish woman who had put her faith in Jesus, while his father was an uncircumcised Greek Gentile.

The believers in both Lystra and Iconium spoke very highly of Timothy's character and faithful service. Even though he was still quite young, he had already earned a fine reputation across the local churches.

Paul wanted Timothy to travel with him as a helper in ministry. Because everyone knew Timothy's father was Greek, Paul circumcised him so Jewish audiences would not be offended or refuse to listen to him preach. Paul did this as a practical step for ministry, not because circumcision is needed for salvation.

As they travelled from town to town, Paul and his companions delivered the guidelines agreed upon by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem. These decisions told Gentile believers they did not have to follow Jewish ritual laws, helping the churches live together in peace.
These clear teachings helped the churches grow firmer and more confident in their faith. Because the believers were united and healthy, more people became Christians every single day.

Paul and his companions travelled through the regions of Phrygia and Galatia because the Holy Spirit stopped them from preaching in the province of Asia at that time. God guided their steps by closing doors until the proper moment arrived.

When the team reached the edge of Mysia, they tried to head north into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them to go there. They willingly submitted to God's direction, trusting that His plans were better than their own.

Since the Holy Spirit kept them from turning north or south, they skirted past Mysia and came down to the port city of Troas on the Aegean coast. God had led them directly to the sea to prepare them for their next assignment.

During the night, Paul was given a vision of a Macedonian man standing and begging him to come across the sea to Macedonia to help them. This vision revealed the deep spiritual hunger and need of the people living across in Europe.

Right after the vision, the group immediately looked for a ship to sail to Macedonia, sure that God was calling them to preach the good news there. The story begins using the word 'we,' showing that Luke, the writer of Acts, had now joined the travel group.
They set sail from Troas and had a smooth, direct voyage across the sea to the island of Samothrace. The following day they reached the harbor town of Neapolis.

From the port, they travelled inland to Philippi, an important city and Roman colony in that district of Macedonia. A Roman colony was like a little piece of Rome itself, with special legal rights for its citizens. They stayed there for several days waiting for the right moment to share their message.

On the Sabbath day, the missionaries went outside the city gate to a riverbank where people usually gathered to pray. Because there was no synagogue in Philippi, only a small group of women had gathered, and Paul and his friends sat down and shared the gospel with them.

One of the listeners was Lydia, a businesswoman from Thyatira who sold expensive purple fabric and was already a worshiper of God. As she listened to Paul, the Lord opened her heart so she could understand and receive the message of salvation.

differ.view: God must sovereignly regenerate and open an unbeliever's heart before that person has any ability to believe the gospel.
God's enabling grace works alongside a person's willingness to seek Him, empowering them to freely choose to accept the truth.

notes.meaning: Lydia and the members of her household were baptized into Christ. She then urged the missionaries to stay as guests in her home, showing immediate generosity and hospitality as a fruit of her new faith.

differ.view: The baptism of a believer's household follows the biblical pattern of God including the children of believers in His covenant family.

notes.meaning: As Paul and his friends were heading back to the place of prayer, they met a young slave girl who had an evil spirit that told fortunes. Her owners earned a large amount of money by charging people for her predictions.

The girl followed behind Paul and the others, shouting that they were servants of the Most High God telling people the way to be saved. Even though her words were true, she spoke by an evil spirit trying to cause disruption and confuse the people.

She kept shouting like this for many days until Paul became deeply grieved and troubled. Turning around, he commanded the demon in the name of Jesus Christ to leave her, and the spirit came out of her that very moment.

When the slave girl's owners saw that their way of making easy money was gone, they became furious. They seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the crowded public marketplace before the city rulers.

The owners brought them to the Roman magistrates and claimed that these Jewish men were causing massive turmoil throughout the city. They concealed their real anger over lost income behind an excuse about public peace.

They charged Paul and Silas with teaching religious practices that were illegal for Roman citizens to accept or observe. Roman law forbade introducing unauthorized religions, so the owners used local civic pride to stir up hatred against the missionaries.

The crowd joined in the angry uprising against Paul and Silas. Without giving them a chance to defend themselves, the magistrates ordered their clothes to be torn off and commanded officers to beat them with wooden rods.
After giving them many painful lashes, the authorities threw Paul and Silas into prison. They strictly charged the jailer to guard them with extreme care so they could not escape.
Carrying out this strict command, the jailer pushed them into the deepest, darkest cell in the prison. He then clamped their feet into heavy wooden stocks that stretched their legs painfully apart.

Around midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns of praise to God despite their bleeding wounds. Their deep joy in God filled the dungeon, and the other prisoners were wide awake, listening to them.
Suddenly a violent earthquake shook the very foundations of the prison house. All the cell doors flew open at once, and every prisoner's heavy chains dropped loose.

The jailer woke up startled and saw the prison doors standing wide open. Believing the prisoners had run away, he drew his sword to kill himself, because Roman guards were put to death if their prisoners escaped.

Paul shouted into the dark with a loud voice, urging the jailer not to harm himself because every single prisoner was still there. Instead of trying to flee, Paul acted with love to protect the life of his guard.
The jailer called for lights, rushed into the cell, and fell down trembling before Paul and Silas. Shaken by the earthquake and amazed by their mercy, he realized that God was with these men.
He led them out of the cell and asked them with deep urgency what he must do to be saved. He knew his soul was in danger and humbly turned to the missionaries to find peace with God.

Paul and Silas told him to place his trust in the Lord Jesus, promising that he and his entire household would be saved. Salvation is a free gift given to anyone who relies on Christ rather than their own efforts.
Paul and Silas then explained God's message of salvation to the jailer and to everyone living under his roof. They made sure the whole family understood who Jesus was and what it meant to follow Him.
Late as it was, the jailer tenderly washed the dried blood from their wounds. Without delay, he and all his household members were baptized as followers of Christ.

differ.view: The baptism of the entire home shows God welcoming a believer's family into the visible covenant community.

notes.meaning: The jailer brought Paul and Silas up into his home and set a warm meal before them. He and his entire family were filled with great joy because they had all come to trust in God.

When daylight arrived, the city magistrates sent their officers to the prison with an order to release Paul and Silas. The rulers likely felt uneasy about the midnight earthquake or realized they had acted unfairly.
The jailer happily reported the news to Paul, telling him that the magistrates had sent word to set them free. He encouraged them to go on their journey in peace.

Paul refused to sneak away, pointing out that the magistrates had beaten Roman citizens in public without a trial and thrown them into prison. He demanded that the rulers come themselves to lead them out, in order to clear their names and protect the new believers in town.

The officers reported Paul's words back to the magistrates, who became terrified when they learned the prisoners were Roman citizens. Under Roman law, beating a citizen without a proper trial was a serious crime that brought severe punishment.

The magistrates came to the prison in person to apologize and escort Paul and Silas out into the open. Because they feared further riots from the crowd, they politely begged the missionaries to leave the city.

After leaving the prison, Paul and Silas went directly to Lydia's house, where the newly converted believers were gathered. They encouraged and comforted these brothers and sisters before departing on their journey.
